findings.description: The skip condition is too broad. `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any placeholder, not just hex escapes. SafeSelector also replaces attribute selectors (`[attr=x]`), `:nth-child(...)` arguments and non-hex escapes such as `\:`. If any of these precedes a real descendant space and the next compound starts with a hex-looking character (a-f or 0-9), the separator is skipped. Examples are `.hover\:bg-blue .bar`, `.md\:flex .container` and `[a] .b`. The two selector parts are then merged and only the last one is scoped, so the earlier part never gets the `[contenta]` attribute. This is a regression in view-encapsulation scoping. The check should be limited to placeholders that stand for a hex escape.

The lookahead uses `selector[res.index + 1]` for every separator type, but the separator regex also matches `+`, `~` and `>>>`. For a combinator without a following space, such as `.\fc+bar`, the char after the combinator is a hex char, so the combinator is wrongly treated as part of an escape sequence and skipped. The check is only meaningful when the separator is a literal space.

The check `part.match(_placeholderRe)` only tests whether the part contains any placeholder. It does not test that the part ends with an escaped character. SafeSelector also uses `__ph-N__` placeholders for attribute selectors such as `[hidden]` and for `:nth-child(...)` expressions. A real descendant combinator after one of these is then wrongly treated as an escape-terminating space whenever the next character is a hex digit or a letter a-f. Examples are `[hidden] div`, `[type=x] button` and `.a\:b .cd`. The separator is skipped and the two compound selectors are scoped as one part, so the first compound loses its `[contenta]` attribute. This changes the scoped output and can leak styles or alter specificity compared with before.

The `if (_global.beforeEach)` / `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. `@angular/core/testing` is imported in environments without a test framework, for example server-side code, utility scripts, or an import before jasmine/mocha is loaded. In those cases it now throws a ReferenceError. This is a regression for existing users, and the old guarded behavior was intentionally safe.

`beforeEach(...)` is now called unconditionally at module load, and `expect` is captured at that point. Without the previous `window`/`global` lookup and `_global.expect` access, importing this module where jasmine globals are not yet defined throws a ReferenceError. The module-level `expect as any` is also evaluated eagerly, so a framework that replaces `expect` later leaves the exported alias stale.

The `_global` export and its private re-export `ɵ_global` were removed from `@angular/localize`. This is a breaking change for any consumer or other package that imports `ɵ_global`, such as tooling or tests. Within this PR only `init` was updated, so other usages could fail to compile.

The old code guarded the hook registration with `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)`. The new code calls `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` unconditionally. Importing `@angular/core/testing` where no test framework has defined these globals now throws a ReferenceError at module load. Examples are a bundler or tooling context, or a runner that only defines `beforeEach`. This is a behavior regression in a refactor labelled as having no functional changes.

`isDefaultImport` returns true only when `importClause.namedBindings` is undefined. For a combined import such as `import CmpA, {CmpB} from './x'`, `namedBindings` is defined, so the default-imported `CmpA` is treated as a named import. The generated deferred loader then reads `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. The check should also look at `importClause.name`. It also ignores type-only or other import clause forms, and it is true for a default import only by accident of the absent named bindings.

isDefaultImport only checks that `namedBindings === undefined`. For a mixed import such as `import CmpA, {Other} from './a'`, the default binding `CmpA` has `namedBindings` defined, so the function returns false. The generated dynamic import then uses `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. The check also ignores which binding the deferred symbol actually comes from. For example, with `import Def, {Named}`, `Named` and `Def` get the same result.

The condition for subscribing to NavigationEnd looks inverted. With no `queryParamsHandling` on the link, it subscribes only when the router's `defaultQueryParamsHandling` is not 'merge' or 'preserve'. So a link that relies on a router default of 'merge' or 'preserve' never subscribes, and its href goes stale after navigation. Meanwhile links that don't depend on router state subscribe needlessly.

The constructor calls `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary()` only when `!this.isAnchorElement`, but that method returns immediately for non-anchor elements. The call is dead code and the condition is inverted. Subscription for anchors now depends entirely on `ngOnChanges`, so an anchor that never gets `ngOnChanges` will never update its href on navigation.

The constructor condition is inverted. It was `if (isAnchorElement) { subscribe } else { setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0') }`. It is now `if (!isAnchorElement) { subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary() } else { setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0') }`. The subscribe call returns immediately for non-anchor elements, so it does nothing. Anchor elements therefore get `tabindex=0` set and no NavigationEnd subscription from the constructor. Non-anchor elements such as `<div routerLink>` no longer get a default tabindex, which breaks keyboard accessibility.

The subscription condition for default query params handling looks backwards. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(options?.defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes when the default does not depend on router state. It skips subscribing when the global default is 'merge' or 'preserve', which is exactly when the href depends on the current router state's query params. In that case the href goes stale after navigation.

The helper replaces `toPromise()` with `first()`, which changes behavior in two ways. An observable that completes without emitting used to resolve `undefined`, but now it rejects with `EmptyError`. For example, a `redirectTo` function or `loadChildren` that returns `EMPTY` used to reach the `if (!cfg) throw canLoadFails(route)` handling, but now throws an unexpected `EmptyError`. An observable that emits several values before completing used to resolve with the last value (`toPromise` semantics), but now resolves with the first. Existing users of such observables could therefore see different results.

cancelLeavingNodes treats any leaving element in a different DOM parent as an overlay duplicate and force-removes it. `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance of a component or template. If one instance is leaving in parent X while a new instance of the same component is inserted in parent Y (for example two list hosts, or a different place in the page), the leaving element is cancelled and removed immediately. Its leave animation is cut short even though it is not a duplicate.

trackLeavingNodes is now called on every Detach for any tNode that has a leave animation. It runs even when animations are disabled or the leave animation is skipped, and in that case clearLeavingNodes is never called. The element then stays in `leavingNodes` indefinitely. These stale, detached elements leak memory and are re-evaluated on every later insert. Moves that detach and re-insert a node are also tracked as leaving.

The code that removed pending enter animations from the animation queue when the same node is detached before the queue ran (removeAnimationsFromQueue) was deleted. Queued enter animations can now still run on an element that has already started its leave animation or been removed. This can cause conflicting enter and leave classes or listeners to fire on a leaving element, such as an `@if` toggled twice quickly within one change detection cycle.

`cancelLeavingNodes` force-removes any leaving element under the same tNode whose parent differs from the new element's parent. A tNode is shared by every instance of a template or component, so unrelated instances in different DOM parents share it. For example, a component with `animate.leave` on its root is used in several containers. When one instance is removed and animating out, creating another instance elsewhere cancels the first one's leave animation and removes it from the DOM immediately. This is a regression that breaks leave animations in ordinary non-overlay layouts.

On every Detach where the tNode has leave animations, the element is tracked in `leavingNodes`. This happens before it is known that a leave animation will actually run, and it also covers detaches that are part of a move or reorder. The element is not cleared on the move path. A live, re-inserted node can therefore stay in `leavingNodes`, and a later insert whose previousSibling is that node would treat it as leaving. That would dispatch a cancel and call `removeChild` on a visible element. The stale entries are also never cleaned up, which leaks them.

The code that removed a node's pending enter animations from the animation queue when its leave animation starts is gone. An element toggled off before the queued enter animation flushes will still have the enter function run against an element that is leaving or already removed. That can apply stale enter classes or listeners to the leaving element and conflict with its leave animation.

The old code interpolated `position` (a number[]) into a string template, so the backend received the comma-separated form "0,1,2". `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now passes the JSON string "[0,1,2]" instead. The backend's `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` appear to parse positions with `split(',').map(parseInt)`. That would give NaN for "[0" and "2]", so view source and select DOM element would fail to find the node. This diff does not change the receiving side, so the format change breaks both operations. The same applies to `selectDomElement` on line 26.

The old template interpolated the ElementPosition array as a comma-joined string, e.g. '0,1,2'. The receiving functions (findConstructorByPosition and findDomElementByPosition) most likely parse it with split(',') and parseInt. stringifyAndEscape now sends the literal string "[0,1,2]", so the first and last indices parse as NaN, because parseInt('[0') is NaN. As a result viewSource and selectDomElement would resolve the wrong node or fail. The diff does not change the receiving side to JSON.parse the argument.
